additions.title: Choose a membrane for the impurity being removed
paragraphs: The supplied slides distinguish separation by particle size and by the type of dissolved material. Microfiltration removes suspended particles and many bacteria but is not a desalination process. Ultrafiltration separates larger dissolved or colloidal material. Nanofiltration can retain multivalent ions and some organic contaminants, while reverse osmosis is used for removing dissolved salts.

Choose the process by the water-quality objective; a general statement that every membrane removes all impurities is not justified. The pore-size and operating-pressure ranges in slides are illustrative rather than universal specifications. Source unit symbols and ranges need a separate visual check before copying a numerical table.

additions.title: Why a small anode attached to a large cathode is vulnerable
paragraphs: The additional handout explains that a large cathodic region can support the cathodic reaction while metal dissolution is concentrated in a much smaller anodic region. The damage is therefore concentrated at the small anode.

When explaining the area effect, identify which region is anodic, which is cathodic and how they are electrically connected through an electrolyte. Comparing metal areas without specifying these roles does not explain the corrosion mechanism.

additions.title: What the additional cracking slides contribute
paragraphs: The slides emphasise improved contact between feed and catalyst, uniform temperature and efficient heat transfer in the described fluidised-bed process. They also identify catalyst regeneration and reuse as advantages. These points can supplement the existing reactor–cyclone–regenerator explanation.

The supplied slide 11 uses “fluidised-bed” and “moving-bed” together. Preserve that course-source terminology when citing the handout, but do not treat it as a universal equivalence between every process bearing those names. A process diagram must be checked against the mechanism actually being described.

additions.title: Explain the roles of fibre and matrix separately
paragraphs: The fibres carry load and provide much of the composite stiffness and strength. The matrix holds the fibres in position and alignment, protects them during manufacture and use, and distributes load among them. These complementary roles explain why an FRP is described as a composite rather than simply a plastic containing loose fibres.

The supporting slides identify carbon-, glass- and aramid-fibre systems and show structural retrofitting applications. Use those examples to explain classification and applications; detailed manufacturing or structural-design procedures are supplementary to the current Chemistry syllabus.
